title: GOD DIDN’T ASK ADAM, “WHY ARE YOU NAKED?” HE ASKED, “WHO TOLD YOU?”
paragraphs: GOD DIDN’T ASK ADAM, “WHY ARE YOU NAKED?” HE ASKED, “WHO TOLD YOU?”
The First Time Humanity Hid in Shame—and the Heartbreaking Reason God Came Looking Anyway | Genesis 3:7–11
Before Adam ever learned how to hide from God, he had already forgotten what it felt like to stand before Him without shame.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part of the story isn't that Adam was hiding.
It's that the God who knew exactly what Adam had done still came looking for him.
Imagine it.
The garden is quiet.
The leaves are moving gently in the breeze. The trees are standing where they have always stood. Everything looks familiar.
But something has changed.
Two human beings who once walked in the presence of their Creator without fear are now crouching among the trees, trying desperately not to be seen.
Their hearts are racing.
Their innocence is gone.
Their hands have been busy sewing leaves together, trying to cover something they have never felt the need to cover before.
And then comes a voice.
The same voice that gave them life.
The same God whose presence had once been their delight.
But now, instead of running toward Him, they hide.
And God asks a question that has echoed through the centuries.
“Who told thee that thou wast naked?” — Genesis 3:11, KJV
Read that again.
Who told you?
Not simply, "Why are you naked?"
Not, "How could you disappoint Me?"
But, "Who told you that you were naked?"
And buried inside that question is a truth that reaches far beyond the Garden of Eden.
Because some of us are still hiding behind leaves we stitched together years ago.
Some of us are still living under the weight of what happened, what we did, what someone said, or what we have become convinced we can never escape.
And the God who called to Adam is still the God before whom nothing is hidden.
But before we turn His question into a comforting slogan, we need to understand what Scripture actually says.
Because this story is more serious, more devastating, and ultimately more hopeful than we sometimes realize.
In Genesis 2:25, before the serpent's deception and before the forbidden fruit, Scripture tells us:
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.”
The original Hebrew says:
וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ
Velo yitboshashu.
“And they were not ashamed.”
That last word comes from the Hebrew root בושׁ (bôsh), associated with shame, disgrace, or being put to shame.
Adam and Eve were naked.
Completely exposed.
Nothing concealed.
Yet there was no shame.
Their nakedness was not a defect. Their bodies were not something sinful. They were God's creation, living in the goodness of what He had made.
There was no guilt to conceal, no disobedience to excuse, no broken trust to fear.
And then Genesis 3 happens.
The serpent questions God's word. Eve sees that the forbidden tree is desirable. She takes its fruit and eats. Adam, who is with her, also eats.
And immediately, something changes.
Genesis 3:7 records:
“And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons.” — KJV
The Hebrew begins:
וַתִּפָּקַחְנָה עֵינֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם
Vattippaqachnah einei sheneihem.
“Then the eyes of both of them were opened.”
But notice the terrible irony.
They had been promised something greater.
The serpent had told Eve that eating would open their eyes and make them like God, knowing good and evil (Genesis 3:5).
Their eyes did open.
But the first thing Scripture tells us they recognized was their nakedness.
The knowledge they sought did not make them sovereign.
It left them painfully aware of their vulnerability.
The text does not say their bodies suddenly became evil. It does not say that nakedness itself was sin.
It says they recognized their nakedness and immediately tried to cover themselves.
And that is where the first human attempt to conceal shame begins.
They reached for fig leaves before they ever answered to God.
Can you picture it?
Adam gathering leaves.
Eve trying to fasten them together.
Two people who had known perfect fellowship with their Creator now desperately attempting to make themselves presentable.
The leaves were real.
The covering was real.
But the deeper problem remained.
They had disobeyed the God who gave them everything.
They could cover their bodies.
They could not undo their rebellion.
And if that doesn't sound painfully familiar, consider how often we do the same thing.
We make a terrible decision and then work harder to appear respectable.
We wound someone and then become defensive rather than confess.
We struggle with secret sin while carefully maintaining a public image of spiritual strength.
We smile in church, say we are blessed, share Bible verses, and make sure no one suspects what has been happening behind closed doors.
Sometimes the leaves look like religious activity.
Sometimes they look like perfectionism.
Sometimes they look like excuses.
Sometimes they look like a carefully edited life on social media.
And sometimes they look like the words:
"I'm fine."
Even when we are not.
There is a difference, of course, between wise privacy and sinful concealment. Not every private struggle belongs before a public audience.
But we know when we are no longer simply protecting something personal.
We are protecting a lie.
We are avoiding repentance.
We are afraid that if the truth comes out, everything will fall apart.
And that fear can become a prison.
You can be surrounded by people and still feel profoundly alone.
You can receive compliments while privately wondering what those same people would think if they knew everything.
You can sing about God's mercy while struggling to believe that mercy could reach you.
And eventually, you can become so accustomed to hiding that you forget what it means to be honest before God.
That is why the next scene in Genesis is so devastating.
Genesis 3:8 says Adam and Eve heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden, and they hid themselves among the trees.
Think about that.
The trees God created became the hiding place of people who had sinned against Him.
The gifts of creation were being used as cover from the Creator.
And then God called to the man:
“Where art thou?” — Genesis 3:9, KJV
The Hebrew is only one word:
אַיֶּכָּה
Ayyekkah.
“Where are you?”
Now we must be careful here.
God was not searching because He lacked information.
Scripture teaches that nothing is hidden from His sight (Hebrews 4:13).
He knew where Adam was.
He knew what had happened.
He knew what they had eaten.
The question was not evidence of divine ignorance.
It was the beginning of a divine confrontation.
God was summoning Adam to answer.
And notice what Adam said.
“I heard thy voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself.” — Genesis 3:10, KJV
There it is.
"I was afraid."
Three words that tell us something had gone terribly wrong.
The man who once enjoyed God's presence now feared it.
The one who had nothing to conceal now hid.
The one who had been unashamed now felt exposed.
Sin had not made God less holy.
It had changed humanity's relationship to Him.
And then comes the question.
The one we cannot afford to rush past.
“Who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?” — Genesis 3:11, KJV
The Hebrew reads:
מִי הִגִּיד לְךָ כִּי עֵירֹם אָתָּה
Mi higgid lekha ki eirom attah?
“Who told you that you were naked?”
The verb הִגִּיד (higgid) comes from a Hebrew root meaning to tell, declare, or make known.
But here is an important distinction.
God was not necessarily asking Adam to identify a person who had spoken a negative message over him.
The verse does not say Satan whispered, "You are worthless."
It does not say Eve insulted Adam.
And it does not teach that Adam's problem was merely poor self-esteem.
God's next question explains the direction of His interrogation:
"Have you eaten of the tree?"
In other words, Adam's new awareness of nakedness was connected to his disobedience.
God was confronting the sin behind the hiding.
And that makes the passage far more searching than a simple message about ignoring negative opinions.
Because sometimes the voice we need to confront is not someone else's criticism.
Sometimes it is our own conscience, troubled because we have genuinely done wrong.
Sometimes our shame is tangled together with guilt that needs confession.
Sometimes the answer is not simply, "Stop feeling bad about yourself."
Sometimes the answer is, "Come into the light. Tell the truth. Turn back to God."
And that is where grace becomes so beautiful.
Because the God who confronted Adam did not cease to be holy.
And the God who is holy did not cease to be merciful.
Both truths matter.
We cannot appreciate the Gospel if we minimize sin.
And we cannot understand the heart of God if we forget His mercy.
But there is another heartbreaking detail in this story.
When God asks Adam about the forbidden fruit, Adam does not simply confess.
He says:
“The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat.” — Genesis 3:12, KJV
Do you hear it?
"The woman..."
And then:
"Whom Thou gavest..."
Adam acknowledges eating, but he also points toward Eve and, indirectly, toward God.
The man who should have taken responsibility begins shifting blame.
Eve, when questioned, points to the serpent's deception.
And suddenly the garden is filled with something humanity still knows too well.
Excuses.
Accusations.
Fear.
Broken trust.
Sin does not merely produce shame.
It damages relationships.
It teaches us to protect ourselves at someone else's expense.
It makes confession difficult because confession requires us to stop defending the image we have constructed.
And maybe that is where this story finds you.
Not hiding behind a tree.
But hiding behind an explanation.
You know you were wrong, but you keep replaying what someone else did first.
You know you need to apologize, but pride keeps telling you to wait.
You know the relationship needs honesty, but fear keeps you silent.
You know the habit is destroying your peace, but you have become skilled at explaining why you cannot stop.
You know God is calling you to repentance, but you are still gathering leaves.
And perhaps the hardest thing to admit is that you have become exhausted trying to maintain a version of yourself that cannot survive the truth.
But listen carefully.
The answer to the shame of Eden was never going to be better fig leaves.
It had to be something only God could provide.
Genesis 3 does not end with Adam and Eve successfully repairing what they broke.
There are real consequences.
The serpent is cursed.
Human life becomes marked by pain, conflict, toil, and death.
Adam and Eve are eventually sent out of Eden.
God's mercy does not erase the seriousness of rebellion.
Yet right there, in the middle of judgment, Scripture gives us a promise that Christians have long understood as pointing toward the coming victory of Christ.
In Genesis 3:15, God speaks of the offspring of the woman and the conflict with the serpent.
The Hebrew uses the word:
זֶרַע
Zera.
“Seed” or “offspring.”
God announces that the woman's offspring will strike the serpent's head, while the serpent strikes his heel.
Within the unfolding story of Scripture, this promise points us toward Jesus Christ, the One who came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8).
It is not a promise that human beings will save themselves by becoming stronger.
It points toward God's answer to the ruin of sin.
And then Genesis 3:21 gives us another remarkable moment:
“Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them.” — KJV
Read that slowly.
God clothed them.
The very people who had disobeyed Him.
The very people who had hidden from Him.
The very people who had tried to cover themselves.
God made garments for them.
We should not claim more than the text reveals. Genesis does not explicitly describe an animal sacrifice here, nor does it directly call these garments an act of atonement.
But it does show something beautiful and unmistakable.
God provided clothing for the people who had failed to cover their situation adequately on their own.
Even in judgment, He acted with care.
And when we follow the whole biblical story forward, we discover that God's provision reaches its fullness in someone far greater than a garment.
Jesus Christ.
The second Adam.
The One who came to do what the first Adam failed to do.
Romans 5:19 declares:
“For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.” — KJV
The contrast is breathtaking.
Adam disobeyed in a garden.
Jesus submitted to the Father's will in Gethsemane.
Adam reached for what God had forbidden.
Jesus refused to abandon the obedience the Father required.
Adam hid after sinning.
Jesus, who had no sin, willingly stepped forward to suffer for sinners.
And at Calvary, something happened that should stop every one of us in our tracks.
The Son of God was stripped.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Exposed to public humiliation.
Soldiers divided His garments.
The sinless Savior endured the shame of crucifixion.
Not because He had committed some secret wrong.
Not because He deserved condemnation.
But because He had come to save the guilty.
Hebrews 12:2 says that Jesus endured the cross, “despising the shame,” and is seated at the right hand of God's throne.
The Greek expression is:
αἰσχύνης καταφρονήσας
Aischynēs kataphronēsas.
“Despising the shame,” or regarding its disgrace as something not worthy of turning Him away from His mission.
Jesus did not pretend the cross was painless.
He did not deny its humiliation.
He endured it.
For the joy set before Him.
And this is where Eden and Calvary meet in a way that should bring us to our knees.
In Eden, guilty humanity tried to cover its shame. At Calvary, the innocent Christ endured shame to redeem the guilty.
That is the Gospel.
Not that our sins were insignificant.
Not that shame can simply be wished away.
Not that God lowered His standards because He felt sorry for us.
But that Jesus Christ bore our sins in His body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24), died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and rose again on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
He did what no amount of human effort could accomplish.
He opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
And this is why you must not confuse conviction with hopeless condemnation.
The Holy Spirit convicts us of sin and points us toward the truth of Christ (John 16:8–14).
But the Gospel does not leave repentant believers trapped under an endless sentence of rejection.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.” — KJV
In the Greek, the word for condemnation is:
κατάκριμα
Katakrima.
A judicial sentence of condemnation.
Paul is not saying believers never feel regret.
He is not saying Christians no longer need to repent.
He is not saying consequences magically disappear.
He is announcing that those who belong to Christ are no longer under the condemning verdict their sins deserve.
That is not cheap comfort.
That is costly grace.
Grace purchased through the blood of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps you need to hear that distinction today.
Because some of you are carrying shame for sins you have already confessed and turned away from.
You keep returning to the same memory.
The same failure.
The same terrible decision.
You have asked God for forgiveness, but you still punish yourself as though suffering long enough might finally make you worthy of mercy.
You keep rehearsing what happened.
You keep imagining what your life would have been if you had chosen differently.
You keep calling yourself by the name of your worst mistake.
And while repentance is necessary, endless self-condemnation is not the same as holiness.
If you are in Christ, your identity is not exhausted by your history.
Your sin was real.
The damage may have been real.
The consequences may still require responsibility, restitution, difficult conversations, and patient rebuilding.
But the cross is real too.
And the resurrection is real.
And the mercy of God is not imaginary.
Consider Peter.
He boldly declared his loyalty to Jesus.
Then, when the pressure came, he denied knowing Him three times.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Can you imagine that moment?
The sound of the rooster.
The memory of his own promises.
The crushing realization that he had denied the Lord he loved.
Peter could not blame someone else for the words that came out of his mouth.
He had failed.
Publicly.
Painfully.
But Peter's story did not end in that courtyard.
After His resurrection, Jesus restored Peter and commissioned him to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
The Lord did not pretend the denial never happened.
He confronted Peter with a searching question about love and called him forward into faithful service.
That is what grace does.
It does not rewrite history by calling evil good.
It rewrites the future by redeeming sinners who could never save themselves.
And perhaps that is why you are still reading.
Because somewhere beneath the responsibilities, the routines, the carefully maintained smile, and the words you use to reassure everyone else, there is a part of you that is tired.
Tired of hiding.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of remembering.
Tired of wondering whether God could possibly use someone with your history.
Maybe you are the believer who fell back into the very sin you promised you would never commit again.
Maybe you are the parent carrying regret over words you cannot take back.
Maybe you are the husband or wife who knows an apology is overdue.
Maybe you are the young person who has allowed a secret struggle to convince you that God must be disgusted with you.
Maybe you were deeply wounded by someone else's sin, and shame has attached itself to you even though you were not responsible for what happened.
If that last sentence describes you, hear this clearly: another person's wrongdoing is not your guilt to carry. What was done to you does not make you less valuable before God.
And if you are the one who sinned, hear this too: the way forward is not denial, but repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
There is room at the cross for truth.
For tears.
For confession.
For wounded people who need healing.
For guilty people who need forgiveness.
For believers who need to return to the Lord.
For those who have spent years assuming they are beyond redemption.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
Notice what John does not say.
He does not say, "If we hide our sins successfully."
He does not say, "If we convince everyone we are righteous."
He does not say, "If we punish ourselves enough."
He says:
"If we confess."
The Greek word is:
ὁμολογῶμεν
Homologōmen.
“If we confess” or “acknowledge.”
It carries the idea of openly acknowledging what is true.
God is not asking us to perform a more convincing version of righteousness.
He calls us to come into the light.
And because of Jesus Christ, confession is not the end of hope.
It is part of walking in the truth before the God who forgives.
You do not need to expose every intimate detail of your life to strangers to prove you are repentant. But you do need to stop treating concealment as a substitute for obedience.
If you have wronged someone, take responsibility.
If you need help overcoming destructive patterns, seek wise, trustworthy support.
If you have been living in deliberate disobedience, turn from it.
If you have wandered from Christ, return to Him.
If you have never trusted Jesus as Savior and Lord, come to Him in repentance and faith.
Not because you have finally made yourself clean.
But because He is the Savior who cleanses sinners.
And here is the question I want you to sit with tonight.
When Adam said, "I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself," he was describing more than an embarrassing moment.
He was revealing what sin had done to his fellowship with God.
Now ask yourself:
What have I been hiding?
What truth am I afraid to acknowledge?
What excuse have I repeated so often that I have begun to believe it?
What shame have I allowed to define me more deeply than the promises of God?
And what would obedience look like if I stopped hiding today?
Maybe it begins with a quiet prayer.
Not a polished prayer.
Not a performance.
Just the truth.

"Lord Jesus, I have been hiding. I have tried to cover things I should have confessed. I have carried shame that I do not know how to release. Forgive my sins. Teach me to repent sincerely. Heal what is wounded. Give me courage to make right what I can. Help me trust what You accomplished through Your death and resurrection. I do not want to keep running from the One who came to save me. Amen."
And if this message has exposed something in your heart, I want to invite you to respond with honesty.
You do not have to explain the details of your pain publicly.
A simple request for prayer is enough.
Someone reading quietly may need to know that the mercy of Jesus Christ is not just a theological idea.
It is the hope by which real sinners are saved and changed.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Not someone you want to accuse.
Someone you genuinely love.
Someone who has been unusually quiet.
Someone who has drifted away from church.
Someone who is struggling to believe that forgiveness is possible.
Someone who has spent years wearing a smile while carrying a hidden burden.
Because there may come a night when an old memory returns, when guilt feels overwhelming, or when you are tempted to run back into hiding.
On that night, return to the Scriptures.
Return to the truth.
Return to the cross.
And remember that Jesus Christ did not come to congratulate the self-righteous.
He came to call sinners to repentance (Luke 5:32).
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not merely to publish words that stir emotion for a few minutes.
Not to collect religious reactions and then leave people spiritually hungry.
But to keep pointing people toward the Word of God, the person and work of Jesus Christ, genuine repentance, grace, forgiveness, and the kind of transformation that only God can accomplish.
There are people who will never walk into a church building simply because someone invited them.
But they may read a Scripture-centered message shared by someone they trust.
And that message may become one of the ways God draws them to hear the Gospel.
These resources are meant to help people move beyond momentary inspiration into a deeper, more consistent relationship with the Lord.
It is a practical way to stand behind the ongoing work of creating, sharing, and expanding Christ-centered teaching and discipleship resources.
We believe that giving generously to support faithful Christian ministry can be an act of worship and stewardship when it is done freely, prayerfully, and with the desire to honor God.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, God loves a cheerful giver—not one who gives under compulsion.
You can pray.
You can share.
You can encourage someone who is struggling.
You can help put the truth of God's Word in front of someone who desperately needs to hear it.
These items are not the heart of the mission.
Jesus Christ is.
The products are simply another way to encourage faith-centered living, share meaningful reminders of Scripture, and support the ongoing work.
Because we are not trying to build a following that admires Gospel Warrior more than it loves Jesus.
We want to help build a community that knows His Word, treasures His grace, takes sin seriously, and follows Him faithfully.
And now, before this message ends, I want to return to the garden one final time.
Adam is standing before God.
His makeshift covering cannot undo his disobedience.
His excuses cannot change what happened.
The trees cannot protect him from the One who sees everything.
And the question still hangs in the air.
"Who told you that you were naked?"
For Adam, the answer leads directly to the sin he committed.
For us, the question invites serious examination of what we have done, what we have believed, and what we are trying to conceal.
But thank God the biblical story does not end with a frightened man among the trees.
It leads us to another Man.
Jesus Christ.
The sinless Savior who hung upon a tree.
The risen Lord who conquered death.
The Redeemer who calls sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And the day is coming when all who belong to Christ will stand before Him, not because they managed to hide their failures, but because His righteousness and saving grace are sufficient.
Revelation 7:14 speaks of those whose robes have been washed and made white in the blood of the Lamb.
What a beautiful picture of redemption.
Humanity began trying to cover its shame with leaves.
The redeemed stand clothed in garments made white through the Lamb's blood.
Not through their own perfection.
Not through their ability to conceal the past.
But through the saving work of Jesus Christ.
So stop running from the truth.
Stop calling darkness your home.
Stop allowing your worst chapter to become the final definition of your life.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive the mercy of Christ by faith.
And walk forward in the light.
Because the most important question is no longer whether you can make yourself look righteous enough to be accepted.
It is whether you will trust the Savior who alone can make sinners right with God.
Adam hid among the trees because of his sin. Jesus hung upon a tree to save sinners like Adam—and sinners like us.
